sonata-form.short: A three-part plan: an exposition presents themes in two keys, a development unsettles them, and a recapitulation brings them back in the home key.

exposition.short: The opening section of a sonata-form movement or a fugue, where the main material is first presented, in a sonata moving to a second key.

development.short: The middle section of a sonata-form movement, where themes are broken into fragments, combined and sent through unrelated keys.

recapitulation.short: The return of the opening themes in the home key that closes the main structure of a sonata-form movement.

coda.short: Italian “tail”: a closing section after the main structure has ended, sometimes only a few chords, sometimes a second development.

rondo.short: A form in which a main theme, the refrain, returns between contrasting episodes: A–B–A–C–A, or more.

ternary-form.short: Three sections: a first, a contrasting middle, and the first again, often decorated or altered on its return.

binary-form.short: A form in two repeated halves: the first leaves the home key, the second returns. Baroque dances and Scarlatti’s sonatas use it.

theme-and-variations.short: A theme stated, then repeated with changing decoration, harmony, texture or mode, while its outline or bass stays recognisable.

fugue.short: A piece built from one short subject, announced by each voice in turn and then developed through imitation, episodes and returns.

subject.short: The main theme of a fugue, stated alone at the start and returning in every voice; in sonata form, one of the movement’s themes.

answer.short: The second entry of a fugue subject, usually in the dominant, while the first voice carries on with a countersubject.

countersubject.short: A companion melody that accompanies each statement of a fugue subject, so the two lines can be heard together.

episode.short: A passage between statements of the main theme that uses fragments and sequences to change key; found in fugues, rondos and concertos.

stretto.short: Italian “narrow”: close imitation in which a fugue subject enters again before the previous statement has finished.

ritornello.short: Italian “little return”: the orchestral refrain of a Baroque concerto, returning between solo episodes, often in related keys and in pieces.

passacaglia.short: A set of continuous variations over a repeating bass or harmonic pattern, usually in slow triple time.

chaconne.short: Variations over a short repeating bass or chord pattern in triple time, close kin to the passacaglia; a Spanish dance made serious.

scherzo.short: Italian “joke”: a fast movement in triple time, usually with a slower trio, that replaced the minuet in symphonies and quartets.

minuet-and-trio.short: The dance movement of Classical symphonies and quartets: a minuet in three beats, a contrasting trio, then the minuet again.

toccata.short: Italian “touched”: a keyboard showpiece in fast, even running notes that tests the player’s hands.

fantasia.short: A piece that follows the player’s imagination rather than a set form, with sudden changes of speed, texture and key.

prelude.short: A piece that precedes another, or an independent short piece without a set form, often built on one figure or texture.

nocturne.short: A short, lyrical piano piece with a singing melody over a broken-chord accompaniment, a form the Irish composer John Field made popular.

lied.short: German art song for solo voice and piano, setting a poem with equal care for words and accompaniment.

aria.short: A self-contained song for one voice in an opera, oratorio or cantata, where the action pauses for a character’s feeling.

recitative.short: Sung speech: a vocal line that follows the rhythm and pitch of the words, used between arias to carry the story.

symphonic-poem.short: A single-movement orchestral work that tells a story or paints a subject, with its form shaped by the programme.

programme-music.short: Instrumental music tied to a story, picture or poem that the composer published or implied.

concerto.short: A work in which one or more soloists contrast and cooperate with an orchestra, usually in three movements.

tonic.short: The home note of a key and the chord built on it: the point of rest that a piece leaves and returns to.

dominant.short: The fifth note of the scale and the chord on it, which pulls strongly towards the tonic; the usual second key of a major-key exposition.

modulation.short: A change of key within a piece, prepared through shared chords or reached abruptly.

cadence.short: A harmonic formula that closes a phrase, like punctuation: perfect, half, deceptive and plagal cadences are the four standard kinds.

pedal-point.short: A note held or repeated in the bass while the harmonies above it change, usually the tonic or the dominant.

neapolitan-sixth.short: A major chord on the flattened second degree, usually in first inversion, used before a cadence for a sudden dark colour.

augmented-sixth.short: A chord containing an augmented sixth between its outer notes, which expand outward by step to an octave on the dominant.

diminished-seventh.short: A four-note chord stacked in minor thirds, so symmetrical that each note can lead to a different key: the standard sound of sudden instability.

tristan-chord.short: The F–B–D♯–G♯ chord of the Prelude to Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde, whose ambiguous function made it a symbol of strained tonality.

chromaticism.short: The use of notes outside the key’s seven-note scale, so that melodies and chords move by semitones.

atonality.short: Music with no tonic: no single note or chord acts as home, so keys and cadences no longer organise it.

twelve-note-row.short: A fixed ordering of all twelve pitch classes, used as the source of a piece’s melodies and harmonies and varied by inversion and reversal.

modes.short: Scales other than major and minor, each with its own pattern of tones and semitones: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian and others.

whole-tone-scale.short: A six-note scale made only of whole steps, with no leading note and so no clear tonic.

octatonic-scale.short: An eight-note scale alternating tone and semitone, symmetrical, with only three transpositions; Rimsky-Korsakov, Stravinsky and Messiaen use it.

bitonality.short: Two keys sounding at once, as in Stravinsky’s Petrushka chord of C major against F♯ major.

suspension.short: A note held over from one chord into the next, where it clashes, then steps down to resolve.

appoggiatura.short: A dissonant “leaning” note that arrives on a strong beat, unprepared, and moves by step to a chord note.

modal-mixture.short: Borrowing notes or chords from the parallel minor or major, so that a tonic keeps its note but changes its colour.

lament-bass.short: A bass descending by step from the tonic to the dominant, a pattern that has signalled grief since the early seventeenth century.

counterpoint.short: Music made by combining independent melodic lines that fit together, as in fugue and canon.

imitation.short: One voice repeating another’s melody a moment later, at the same pitch or a different one.

canon.short: Strict imitation: a melody followed note for note by other voices entering at a fixed distance; a round is a canon that can repeat endlessly.

homophony.short: A texture in which one line leads and the others support it, often moving in the same rhythm as chords.

ostinato.short: Italian “obstinate”: a short phrase, rhythm or bass pattern repeated persistently while other things change above it.

motif.short: A short musical idea — a few notes with a recognisable rhythm or contour — that a composer repeats and transforms.

leitmotif.short: A theme tied to a person, object or idea in a music drama, returning with changed harmony or orchestration as the story develops.

cyclic-form.short: A work in several movements that brings back the same theme or themes in more than one of them.

orchestration.short: The choice of which instruments play each line; it can change a melody’s colour and weight without changing a note.

divisi.short: Italian “divided”: a string section splits so that its players play different parts instead of the same one.

pizzicato.short: Plucking a string with the finger instead of drawing the bow across it, giving a short, dry note.

tremolo.short: Rapid repetition of one note, on strings by very short bow strokes, to make a shimmering, unsettled sustained sound.

col-legno.short: Italian “with the wood”: string players strike or draw the stick of the bow, not its hair, for a dry, clattering sound.

ornament.short: A small decorative note or group — trill, turn, mordent — added to a melody note, written as a sign or in small notes.

rubato.short: Italian “stolen”: a flexible tempo in which the performer lingers on some notes and hurries others, giving back the time within the phrase.

metre.short: The regular grouping of beats into bars: 3/4 is three crotchet beats to the bar, 6/8 two groups of three quavers.

polyrhythm.short: Two or more conflicting rhythms sounding together, such as two notes in one hand against three in the other.

bar.short: A unit of music between two bar lines, holding a set number of beats; scores number the bars so passages can be found.

catalogue-number.short: The number that identifies a work: Op. for the composer’s or publisher’s opus order, or a letter code from a later scholar’s catalogue.

equal-temperament.short: The tuning that divides the octave into twelve equal semitones, so every key sounds alike and no interval except the octave is perfectly pure.

well-temperament.short: A family of historical tunings in which every key is usable but each has a slightly different colour; not the same as equal temperament.

concert-pitch.short: The frequency to which an orchestra tunes: A=440 Hz today, but Baroque ensembles often tune near A=415, about a semitone lower.

clavichord.short: A small keyboard instrument in which brass tangents strike the strings and stay in contact while the key is held; quiet, but sensitive to touch.

basset-clarinet.short: A clarinet extended downwards by a few notes, for which Mozart wrote his Clarinet Concerto, K. 622, for Anton Stadler.

basso-continuo.short: The accompanying bass line of Baroque music, played by a low melody instrument and a chord player who fills in the harmony from numbers.

period-instruments.short: Instruments built like those of the composer’s day, or copies, played with the pitch, tuning and techniques of the period.

acoustic-recording.short: Recording before microphones, when performers played into a horn that drove the cutting stylus directly; electrical recording replaced it in 1925–27.

78-rpm.short: The nominal speed of shellac discs from the early 1900s to the 1950s; a 12-inch side held about four and a half minutes.

matrix-number.short: The number etched in a disc’s run-out groove that identifies the recording; a take number says which attempt was issued.

transfer.short: Copying a disc or tape into a digital file; the stylus, playback speed, equalisation and noise reduction chosen all shape what you hear.

public-domain-audio.short: Free of copyright. A composition and a recording of it have separate terms, so out-of-copyright music can sit on a protected recording.

level-trace.short: The Hall’s graph of relative level within one recording: where it grows stronger or quieter, never loudness or a comparison between recordings.

score-alignment.short: Matching a score’s bars to times in a recording by software; the Hall marks such timings provisional until a listener has checked them by ear.

quotation.short: Using a recognisable passage of another work, or a chant or tune, inside a new piece, openly or as an allusion.

parody.short: Two senses: in Renaissance and Baroque practice, reworking existing music into a new piece; today, imitation that mocks.

modelling.short: Taking another work’s plan — its form, its bass, its procedure — as the pattern for a new piece, without quoting its notes.

homage.short: A piece made in honour of another composer or person, often in their style or forms; a tombeau is an homage in memory of the dead.

transcription.short: Rewriting a piece for different instruments, from keyboard to orchestra or the reverse; a transcription stays close to the original’s notes.

evidence-status.short: How firmly a connection or fact is supported: documented (a source states it), inferred (the evidence points to it) or disputed (sources disagree).

perfect-cadence.short: The dominant chord followed by the tonic, both in root position: the strongest full stop in tonal harmony.

half-cadence.short: A phrase that ends on the dominant chord, which sounds unfinished and asks for a continuation.

deceptive-cadence.short: A dominant chord that resolves to a chord other than the tonic, usually the minor chord on the sixth degree (V–vi), so the expected close is denied.

plagal-cadence.short: The subdominant chord moving to the tonic (IV–I), the “Amen” cadence: gentler and less final than dominant to tonic.

elision.short: Two phrases or sections overlap, so the last chord of one is also the first of the next and no gap separates them.

pivot-chord.short: A chord that belongs to both the old key and the new one, used as a hinge to modulate smoothly.

common-tone-modulation.short: Moving to a distant key by holding one note shared by both harmonies, which is heard afresh as a different member of the new chord.

direct-modulation.short: Changing key without preparation: a phrase ends in one key and the next simply begins in another.

enharmonic-reinterpretation.short: Respelling a note or chord — D♭ as C♯, say — so that it leads to a different key from the one its first spelling implied.

chromatic-slide.short: Moving a note or chord by a semitone to reach new harmonic ground, without a conventional modulation.

sequence.short: A short melodic or harmonic pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch, usually several times in a row.

dominant-pedal.short: A held or repeated dominant note in the bass: the music waits for the tonic that it promises.

tonic-pedal.short: A held or repeated tonic note in the bass: the harmony moves above it, but the music stays at home.

retransition.short: The passage that prepares the return of the opening material, typically by lingering on the dominant of the home key.

standing-on-the-dominant.short: Holding dominant harmony for a long stretch, so that a return or arrival is delayed and expected.

liquidation.short: Stripping a theme down, motif by motif, until only a fragment or a single chord is left, often before a return.

motivic-link.short: A small motif carried across a join, so the new section feels derived from the old even when key, texture and tempo change.

fermata.short: A sign, an arc over a dot, that holds a note or rest beyond its written length; the performer decides how long.

general-pause.short: Silence for the whole ensemble at once: a deliberate break that stops the music before it restarts.

medial-caesura.short: The pause in a sonata exposition that separates the first group from the second theme, usually after a half cadence on the dominant.

crescendo-build.short: A long, gradual increase in force that carries the music towards a climax, by adding instruments, notes, register or speed.

decrescendo.short: A gradual fall in loudness; at a join it can clear space for the next section or let a climax dissolve.

texture-change.short: A shift in how the parts are layered: solo to ensemble, melody and accompaniment to counterpoint, chords to running notes.

orchestration-change.short: A change in who plays the music — a melody handed to other instruments, a section dropped or added — that marks or shapes the join.

register-change.short: A move into a much higher or lower pitch range, which changes the weight and colour of the music at a join.

tempo-change.short: A shift of speed marked in the score, such as Largo to Moderato, that signals a new section.

metre-change.short: A change of time signature or beat grouping, which alters how the pulse is felt.

link-passage.short: A short passage written to connect two sections: no new theme, only the harmony and motion that lead from one to the other.

cadenza.short: A passage for the soloist alone in a concerto or aria, displaying technique over a pause on the dominant; originally improvised.

attacca.short: Italian “attack”: an instruction to go straight on to the next movement without a pause.

fade.short: An ending in which the music tapers away to nothing instead of closing on a final cadence.
